title: For a 10% blood-volume change in 1 minute, speckle and bone loss limit functional ultrasound through adult parietal bone to about 2.6-3.5 mm voxels, coarser than 3T fMRI in 59-81% of model draws
abstract: Functional ultrasound through the intact adult parietal or frontal skull resolves coarser voxels than 3T functional MRI (fMRI) in most model draws; a thin temporal-bone window usually does better than 3T, but not 7T. This matters because groups and companies now try to put functional ultrasound through the skull: the result shows which sites can work, what to measure first, and how to design the probe. Power Doppler, the usual signal, is the echo power of moving blood. The echo is a random interference pattern (speckle), so noise decreases only with new, independent patterns. Independent patterns per second per mm3 of cortex increase as the fourth power of frequency, while bone loss increases exponentially with frequency (fit to 89 published skull fragments). Each bone thus has an optimum frequency, where blood signal-to-noise is about 1.2 per frame: about 1.9 MHz for 2.5 mm temporal bone, 1.1 MHz for parietal and 0.8 MHz for frontal bone. Over 3000 parameter draws, each paired with its own fMRI values and with physiological noise for both methods, the smallest voxel that detects a 10% blood-volume change (z = 5, 60 s per condition) had a median of 3.5 mm parietal (90% range 1.8-7.5; 1.5 times the 3T voxel), 5.2 mm frontal and 1.7 mm temporal, against 2.3 mm for 3T and 1.2 mm for 7T. Parietal ultrasound beat 3T in 24% of draws (19% where both methods detect). Only 36% of draws reproduce a published deep transcranial detection; in those, parietal reaches 2.6 mm and beats 3T in 41%. The result depends most on in vivo bone attenuation and fMRI quality. Microbubble contrast and localization microscopy are worse at clinical doses: a few large bubbles carry the echo, so contrast matches red-cell Doppler through parietal bone only at about 4 million bubbles per mL of blood. Simulation agreed with the noise model (variance ratio 0.82-1.16). In public rat raw data the measured variance was 1.4-2.5 times the Gaussian speckle prediction, never below it, and gave the decorrelation bandwidth (12.7 Hz per MHz). In public human data per-pixel noise was 4-10 times the speckle floor. An independent review corrected the first version. The measurement that decides the parietal case is in vivo bone loss at 1-2 MHz.

display.caption: A: Independent power-Doppler samples per s per mm3 of cortex against frequency (base parameters). Without bone the rate increases as f^4 (speckle limit); bone loss gives an optimum near 1.9, 1.1 and 0.8 MHz for temporal, parietal and frontal bone. B: Smallest voxel that detects a 10% blood-volume change in 60 s (z = 5) over 3000 draws, with paired 3T (band 10-90%) and 7T fMRI.
